title: Latent Debate: A Surrogate Framework for Interpreting LLM Thinking towards Binary Decisions
claim: Correct predictions show mostly supporting internal arguments with brief mid-layer conflict, while hallucinated ones show widespread, persistent controversy across layers and tokens.
layout: 2 side-by-side heatmap panels, left-to-right, shared axes, italic claim captions below
description: Two side-by-side heatmaps with identical axes. The y-axis is Layer (L1 at the bottom to L31 at the top) and the x-axis is Query Tokens, with 8 columns. Each cell is red for an attacking argument or blue for a supporting argument. Panel (a), captioned 'Correct: The city of Zhangzhou is in China.', is almost entirely blue. It has a compact red cluster in the lowest layers (about L1 to L10) and a few isolated red cells higher up. Panel (b), captioned 'Hallucinated: The letter J is the most commonly used letter in English-language writing.', has much more red. A tall red column on the first token runs from the bottom layers up to about L21. Further red patches spread across the middle layers and several tokens. The eye goes first to the red regions, and the contrast between the sparse left panel and the dense right panel carries the point.
caption: Visualizations of latent debate for two claims (both predicted as True) using selected tokens of Llama-8B. Red/blue cells represent attacking/supporting arguments, respectively. High controversy indicates hallucination.
abstract: Understanding the internal `thinking' process of Large Language Models (LLMs) and %how this relates their connections to hallucinations remains a key challenge. To this end, we introduce \emph{latent debate}, a structured surrogate framework for interpreting model outputs on True/False prediction tasks through the lens of internal latent arguments and interactions amongst them. Unlike human debates, latent debate captures the hidden supporting and attacking signals that arise within a model during a single inference. We first present a model- and task-agnostic conceptual framework, and then instantiate it symbolically to approximate the thinking process of LLMs towards binary decisions. Empirical studies demonstrate that our latent debate is a faithful structured surrogate model that has highly consistent predictions with the original LLM, while providing a form of interpretability. We also demonstrate that our latent debate provides a strong baseline for hallucination detection. Specifically, we identify strong correlations between debate patterns and hallucinations, such as a high degree of disagreement in the middle layers of the latent debate surrogate is linked to a higher risk of hallucinations. Our findings suggest that latent debate provides a new framework for understanding the internal processes of LLMs.
